'''''Sabal palmetto''''' ({{IPAc-en|'|s|eɪ|b|ə|l}}, ''[[Help:Pronunciation respelling key|SAY-bəl]]''), also known as '''cabbage palm''',<ref name="q" /> '''cabbage palmetto''',<ref name="GRIN" /> '''sabal palm''', palmetto palm, blue palmetto,<ref name="GRIN" /> Carolina palmetto,<ref name="USFS">{{Silvics |volume=2 |genus=Sabal |species=palmetto |first1=Dale D. |last1=Wade |first2=O. Gordon |last2=Langdon |access-date=2014-03-22}}</ref> common palmetto,<ref name="USFS" /> and '''swamp cabbage''',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.plantapalm.com/vpe/misc/sabal-palmetto.pdf|title=Cabbage, Swamp — Sabal palmetto (Walt.) Lodd ex Schult. & Schult.f., Fact Sheet HS-571|author=James M. Stephens|publisher=University of Florida, Florida Cooperative Extension Service|year=1994}}</ref> is one of 15 species of [[Sabal|palmetto]] [[Arecaceae|palm]].
It is native to the Southeast United States Coastal Plain, the [[Yucatán Peninsula]] in Mexico, and the [[West Indies]].

==Description==
''Sabal palmetto'' grows up to {{Cvt|80|ft|m|order=flip}} tall, with the tallest on record measuring at 93 feet tall.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sabal Palm |publisher=U.S. National Park Service |url=https://www.nps.gov/places/000/sabal-palm.htm |access-date=2024-04-03 |language=en}}</ref> Starting at half to two-thirds the height, the tree develops into a rounded, costapalmate fan of numerous [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]]. A costapalmate leaf has a definite costa (midrib), unlike the typical palmate or fan leaf, but the leaflets are arranged radially like in a palmate leaf. All costapalmate leaves are about {{Cvt|5|mm|4=1|frac=4}} across, produced in large compound panicles up to {{Cvt|2.5|m|ft|1|frac=2}} in radius, extending out beyond the leaves. The [[fruit]] is a black [[drupe]] about {{Cvt|1.3|cm|frac=2}} long containing a single seed. It is extremely [[Halophyte|salt-tolerant]] and is often seen growing on the coastal plain and along the coast of the [[Atlantic Ocean]] and the [[Gulf of Mexico]].<ref name="q">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200027118 ''Sabal palmetto'']. Flora of North America.</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Sabal palmetto'' is native to the [[Subtropics|subtropical]] coastal regions of the American states of [[Florida]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[South Carolina]], and southeastern [[North Carolina]]. It is also cultivated elsewhere in the [[Southeastern United States|Southeastern US]], in some areas of southeastern [[Virginia]], southwestern [[Alabama]], and southeastern [[Mississippi]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weakley |first=Alan S. |date=24 April 2022 |title=Flora of the Southeastern United States |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/img/flora/FSUS2022.pdf |publisher=University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Herbarium |page=319}}</ref> It can also be found alongside [[Cuba]]'s northern coast (from [[Havana]] to [[Matanzas]]),<ref name="Vandeelen">Van Deelen, Timothy R. 1991. [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/sabpal/all.html Sabal palmetto]. Fire Effects Information System, Forest Service, U.S. Department of Agriculture.</ref> the [[Turks and Caicos Islands|Turks and Caicos]], the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, and [[the Bahamas]].<ref name="Vandeelen" /><ref name="Zona">{{Cite journal |last=Zona |first=S. |year=1990 |title=A monograph of ''Sabal'' (Arecaceae: Coryphoideae) |journal=Aliso |publisher=[[Rancho Santa Ana Botanic Garden]] |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=583–666 |doi=10.5642/aliso.19901204.02 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="bonap">[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Sabal%20palmetto.png 2014 county distribution map]. Biota of North America Program.</ref>

The species is [[Hardiness zone|hardy]] to the [[US Department of Agriculture]]'s zone 8a, and has been reported to have some cold hardness down to {{convert|8.6|F|C|1|disp=or}}, but needs hot and humid summers to grow well. Maintenance of the cabbage palm tree is very easy and very adaptable. The cabbage palmetto is known to [[Drought tolerance|tolerate drought]], standing water and brackish water. Even though this palm is drought-tolerant, it thrives on regular light watering and regular feeding. It is highly tolerant of salt winds, but not saltwater flooding.<ref>{{cite web |title=Real Palm Trees |work=Palm Tree General Description |url=http://realpalmtrees.com/palm-blog/a-e/cabbage-palm-sabal-palmetto/ |access-date=2008-11-23 |archive-date=2010-10-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101025103152/http://realpalmtrees.com/palm-blog/a-e/cabbage-palm-sabal-palmetto/ }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
{{See also|List of hardy palms}}

''Sabal palmetto''<ref name="Southern Research Station">{{Cite web |title=''Sabal palmetto'' (Walt) Lodd. ex J. A. & J. H. Schult. Cabbage Palmetto |url=https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/misc/ag_654/volume_2/sabal/palmetto.htm |access-date=2024-05-23 |publisher=Southern Research Station, Forest Service, USDA}}</ref> is a popular landscape plant in the subtropical climates of the Gulf and south Atlantic states, mostly from coastal regions of North Carolina to Florida.<ref name="Southern Research Station" /><ref name="IFAS Sabal palmetto">{{Cite web |title=ENH-733/ST575: ''Sabal palmetto'': Sabal or Cabbage Palm |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ST575 |access-date=2025-05-22 |website=Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS |language=en}}</ref> Sabal palm is used extensively around beach and resort areas along the lower East Coast because of its tolerance of salt spray and drought.<ref name="IFAS Sabal palmetto" /> Because of their relatively long establishment period and prevalence on southern ranchlands, few, if any are grown from seed in nurseries.<ref name="IFAS Regenerated">{{Cite web |title=ENH1279/EP543: Regenerated Sabal/Cabbage Palms (Sabal palmetto): Why and How |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/EP543 |access-date=2025-05-22 |website=Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS |language=en}}</ref> Instead, established plants are dug in the wild with small rootballs since virtually all the severed roots die and must be replaced by new roots in the new location.<ref name="IFAS Sabal palmetto" /> Most leaves are removed during [[transplanting]] to reduce [[transpiration]]. Cabbage palms have excellent [[Tropical cyclone|hurricane]] resistance, but are frequently overpruned to supposedly lower wind loads.<ref name="IFAS Regenerated" /> Sabal palm seed germination excels in hot and humid summer climates.<ref name="IFAS Sabal palmetto" />

Most references rate the species as hardy to USDA hardiness zone 8b.<ref name="IFAS Sabal palmetto" /> A small number of specimens are cultivated beyond the typical regions sabal is known to be cultivated in, including parts of [[Tennessee]], northern [[Virginia]], and along the middle Atlantic coast from [[Maryland]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Sabal minor'' Dwarf Palmetto |url=https://sheffields.com/seeds-for-sale/Sabal/minor/4816/Dwarf-Palmetto/Dwarf-Palmetto |access-date=2025-05-22 |website=Sheffields Seeds Online Ltd |language=en}}</ref> to coastal [[New Jersey]] and coastal [[Connecticut]]. A long term specimen (covered with frost cloth in winter) grows in favorable microclimate (zone 7a/b) at the [[University of Bridgeport]], Connecticut, since 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://oak.conncoll.edu/notabletrees/ViewTreeData.jsp?selected=226219 |title=View Tree Data - Connecticut's Notable Trees |publisher=Connecticut College |language=en |access-date=1 January 2026}}</ref>

The cabbage palm is remarkably resistant to fire, floods, coastal conditions, cold, high winds, and drought.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cabbage Palmetto |url=https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/misc/ag_654/volume_2/sabal/palmetto.htm |access-date=March 4, 2024}}</ref> Despite this, mortality has been caused by [[Texas phoenix palm decline]] (now known as Lethal Bronzing Disease), a [[phytoplasma]] found on the west coast of Florida in 2006.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PP243/PP163: Lethal Bronzing Disease (LB) |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/PP163 |access-date=2025-05-22 |website=Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS |language=en}}</ref>

''Sabal palmetto'' trunks appear in two different conditions, which can be confusing (see photo). When leaves die, the leaf bases typically persist for a while, creating a spiky, "basketweave" effect. These remnant leaf bases are called "bootjacks" or "boots", for short. The name stems from the "Y" shape that was reminiscent of [[Boot jack|devices used to aid individuals in removing boots]]. Transplanted palms are sometimes deliberately shorn of these bootjacks. Taller specimens are more likely to have lost their bootjacks and appear relatively smooth and columnar. The loss of bootjacks is a natural, if poorly understood, phenomenon, as the palm does not create a leaf [[abscission]] zone so the loss of the leaf bases results from some other physical or biological process.

In 1998, a new mutant form of ''S. palmetto'' was discovered in southwest [[Florida]], and named as a [[cultivar]], ''Sabal palmetto'' 'Lisa'. This cultivar has unusually thick and leathery, largely fused leaflets that give the palm a unique and appealing appearance. Over 60% of the seedlings have the same leaf characteristics as the parent plant and ''Sabal palmetto'' 'Lisa' has been popularized in the nursery trade in Florida over the last 20 years and proven to be as resistant to heat, wind, cold, drought, and neglect as the common form while keeping its shape.<ref>{{cite web |title=A new cultivar of ''Sabal palmetto'' |url=http://www.palms.org/palmsjournal/2005/vol49n1p46-47.pdf |work=Palm Tree General Description |access-date=2010-01-06 |archive-date=2009-07-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708054146/http://www.palms.org/palmsjournal/2005/vol49n1p46-47.pdf }}</ref>

Outside of the United States, sabal palmetto is also cultivated in some areas of the [[Caucasus]] region of [[Eastern Europe]], primarily in cities such as [[Sochi]], [[Sukhumi]], and [[Batumi]], though this is less common than elsewhere and primarily limited to microclimates. It is also grown in some coastal regions of [[Japan]] and [[South Korea]].

== Uses ==
The growing heart of the new fronds, also known as the [[Bud#Types of buds|terminal bud]], gives the tree its "cabbage" name, since this is extracted as a food and tastes like other undifferentiated plant meristem tissue, such as the heart of a cabbage or [[artichoke]]. It is one of several palm species that are sometimes used to make [[heart of palm]] salad. Heart of palm was commonly eaten by [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sabal Palm |publisher=U.S. National Park Service |url=https://www.nps.gov/places/000/sabal-palm.htm |access-date=2024-03-05 |language=en}}</ref> However, extracting the heart kills this species of palm, because the terminal bud is the only point from which the palm can grow, so without this bud, the palm is not able to replace old leaves and eventually dies.

The cabbage-like terminal bud has been eaten as hearts of palm. The bristles on the sheaths of young leaves have been made into scrubbing brushes. The trunks have been used as wharf piles. On June 28, 1776, Charleston patriots under [[William Moultrie]] made a fort of palmetto trunks and from it [[Battle of Sullivan's Island|defended successfully]] against the British in the Revolutionary War.<ref>Peattie, Donald Culross. ''Trees You Want to Know''. Whitman Publishing Company, Racine, Wisconsin, 1934. p. 36.</ref>

The fruit is edible raw, and the seeds can be ground into flour.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |author=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=74 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

==Culture==
The sabal palmetto is the official [[state tree]] of both Florida and South Carolina (the latter is nicknamed "The Palmetto State").

The annual football rivalry game between [[Clemson University|Clemson]] and [[University of South Carolina|South Carolina]] is known as the "Palmetto Bowl".

A [[silhouette]] of ''S. palmetto'' appears on the official [[Flag of South Carolina|flag of the US state of South Carolina]].<ref>[http://www.netstate.com/states/symb/flags/sc_flag.htm Netstate, South Carolina State Flag]</ref> The seal of South Carolina also depicts the sabal palmetto.

An image of a palmetto appears on the back of South Carolina's [[state quarter]], which was issued in 2000.

Two images of ''S. palmetto'' appear on the official [[Seal of Florida|great seal of the State of Florida]]<ref>[http://www.netstate.com/states/symb/seals/fl_seal.htm The Great Seal of the State of Florida]</ref> and the [[flag of Florida]].
